article.headline: S&P Call Skew at Historic Highs as Options Traders Chase Upside
article.lede: The S&P 500 options market has turned itself inside out. Traders are paying record premiums for call options — bets on further gains — while interest in downside protection has sunk to historically low levels, a configuration that options professionals call extreme *call skew*. The result is an unusual regime where *implied volatility* rises alongside stock prices, a dynamic that historically precedes sharp reversals.
article.body:
*Volatility skew* is the premium that options at different strike prices command relative to each other on the same expiry. In normal equity markets, *put options* — contracts that pay off when stocks fall — have carried higher implied volatility than equivalent calls since Black Monday 1987; four decades of institutional demand for crash insurance entrenched the bias. The charts Zero Hedge published show two deviations from that norm. The first tracks the one-year percentile rank of SPX call and put vol skew; by mid-2026, call skew sits near its 99th-plus percentile while put skew is near a floor. The second plots the 3-month **25-delta** call-to-*ATM* ratio for individual stocks back to 2017, now at or near an all-time high — meaning *out-of-the-money* calls are priced nearly as expensively as equivalent puts, an inversion that typically signals speculative fever rather than strategic positioning.

The mechanics driving this are well-documented, if rarely this vivid. When dealers sell call options in bulk, they become *short gamma* — their risk exposure grows as markets rise, forcing them to buy equities and futures to stay *delta-neutral*. That buying lifts prices, which attracts more call buyers, which forces more dealer buying: a self-reinforcing *gamma squeeze*. Nomura (8604.T) cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott has called the current episode “one of the most powerful gamma squeezes ever.” On approximately May 7, 2026, S&P 500 call options traded a record $2.6 trillion in notional value in a single session — the highest ever recorded. Calls accounted for roughly 58% of all SPX options flow, and retail traders, now representing about 53% of *0DTE* (same-day-expiry) SPX options volume, supplied much of the demand.

The trigger is not obscure. The S&P 500 rose more than 10% in April 2026 — its strongest month since late 2020 — as first-quarter earnings came in sharply above expectations: 84% of reporting companies beat estimates by an average of 12.3%, nearly double the historical norm. The artificial-intelligence spending boom has turbocharged the narrative; Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META) collectively guided toward $710 billion in AI infrastructure investment for 2026, and Nvidia (NVDA) captured much of the resulting enthusiasm. Dealers who had been net-short gamma through the Q1 pullback saw their positions flip violently as the rally took hold, amplifying every uptick through forced hedging. Goldman Sachs (GS) strategist Rich Privorotsky summarized the mood tersely: the market has entered “a semi-irrational chasing phase.”

The historical parallels are uncomfortable. The **Shiller CAPE** — a price-to-earnings ratio that averages ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings to smooth out cycles — reached 40.3 in mid-May 2026, a level only previously achieved during the 1999–2000 dot-com peak. That era ended with the S&P 500 shedding 47% over three years. Paul Tudor Jones, in a May 7 television appearance, invoked 1999 explicitly, warning of “breathgaking kinds of corrections” — while disclosing he was still buying AI stocks. The structural risk is as mechanical as it is fundamental: when the record outstanding call positions expire or are closed, the forced dealer buying supporting prices evaporates, and the same hedging math can rapidly reverse into forced selling.

concepts.definition: The difference in implied volatility between options at different strike prices on the same expiry date. In equity markets, options well below the current price (puts) normally carry higher implied volatility than options well above it (calls) — a pattern called put skew. When call skew rises, it means upside options have become unusually expensive, typically reflecting speculative demand rather than hedging.

The market's expectation of future price swings, backed out from current options prices. Higher implied volatility means options buyers are paying more for the chance of large moves. It reflects supply and demand in the options market as much as actual uncertainty, so extreme readings can themselves be a market signal.

Contracts giving the holder the right to sell an asset at a specified price before expiry. For equity investors, puts function as insurance: they pay off when markets fall. Institutional demand for index puts — to protect large equity portfolios — has historically been the structural force behind put skew in index options markets.

Options whose price changes by 25 cents for every $1 move in the underlying — roughly equivalent to being about 5–8% out-of-the-money for typical index options. The 25-delta strike is the standard reference for measuring volatility skew because it captures meaningful tail exposure while remaining liquid enough to trade reliably.

An option whose strike price equals (or is closest to) the current market price of the underlying. ATM options are the most actively traded and serve as the baseline against which skew is measured. The call-to-ATM ratio compares the implied volatility of out-of-the-money calls to ATM options; a ratio approaching 1.0 signals extreme speculative demand for upside.

An option whose strike price has not yet been reached by the underlying asset's price. For a call, OTM means the market is still below the strike; for a put, the market is above it. OTM options cost less than at-the-money ones but provide leverage if the market moves sharply, making them the preferred instrument for directional speculation.

The risk profile of a party — typically a dealer — that has sold options and whose losses accelerate as the market moves against them. A short-gamma dealer must continuously buy into rising markets or sell into falling ones to stay hedged, mechanically amplifying the underlying trend in both directions.

A strategy of balancing an options position with an offsetting stake in the underlying asset so that small price moves produce no net gain or loss. Dealers running delta-neutral books must rebalance constantly as prices shift — this ongoing rebalancing transmits options market imbalances into actual stock-price pressure.

A self-reinforcing feedback loop in which heavy call-option buying forces dealers to purchase the underlying asset to stay hedged, lifting prices further, which attracts more call buyers and forces more hedging. Unlike a short squeeze (which involves borrowed shares), a gamma squeeze operates entirely through the mechanics of options dealer hedging and can accelerate rapidly.

An unusual regime in which equity prices and implied volatility both rise simultaneously. Normally they move inversely — calm markets produce low volatility. When both rise together it signals that options mechanics (forced dealer buying from short-gamma positions) rather than improving fundamentals are driving the move, implying a structurally fragile rally.

Options that expire on the same day they are traded (zero days to expiry). They carry extreme gamma — small price moves can produce large swings in their value — making them powerful amplifiers of intraday market moves. Since 2022 they have become the dominant product in S&P 500 options markets by volume, with retail traders now supplying a majority of the flow.

The Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings ratio, developed by economist Robert Shiller, which divides the S&P 500's current price by ten years of inflation-adjusted average earnings. By smoothing out single-year earnings distortions it offers a longer-horizon valuation gauge. Readings above 40 have historically been rare, appearing only at the height of the 1999–2000 dot-com bubble.

article.fact_check: Zero Hedge's claim that 'nobody has any downside protection' is rhetorical exaggeration. The charts show put vol skew at low but non-zero percentile ranks, and institutional investors still hold put positions as a matter of policy. The substantive point — that relative demand has shifted dramatically from puts to calls, leaving the market asymmetrically exposed to downside — is well-supported by the data.

ticker_8604-t.name: Nomura Holdings, Inc.
ticker_8604-t.blurb: Nomura Holdings is Japan's largest investment bank and brokerage firm, providing a broad range of financial services including retail brokerage, asset management, wholesale banking, and investment banking. Founded in 1925 and headquartered in Tokyo, it operates across Asia, Europe, and the Americas, serving individual investors, corporations, financial institutions, and governments. Nomura is widely regarded as the preeminent Japanese securities house and competes globally with major Western investment banks in fixed income, equities, and advisory services.
ticker_8604-t.recent: As of mid-May 2026, Nomura shares (8604.T) were trading around ¥1,265, near a 52-week low of ¥827 set on May 12, 2025, and well off the 52-week high of ¥1,506.50 reached in January 2026. Price action has been pressured by broader macro uncertainty including U.S.-China trade tensions and geopolitical headwinds affecting Asian financial markets. No company-specific earnings or major corporate announcements are surfaced in the available sources for the past 30 days.

ticker_msft.name: Microsoft Corporation
ticker_msft.description: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.blurb: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.

ticker_amzn.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
ticker_amzn.blurb: Amazon operates the world's largest e-commerce marketplace and the leading cloud infrastructure platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS). AWS generates the majority of Amazon's operating profit despite representing a minority of total revenue. The company also has significant positions in digital advertising, streaming (Prime Video), and logistics infrastructure. Amazon is a major investor in AI, both through AWS cloud AI services and through a multi-billion-dollar strategic stake in Anthropic.
ticker_amzn.recent: Amazon reported FY2025 revenue exceeding $650 billion, with AWS growing at roughly 17% annually and crossing $100 billion in run-rate revenue. The advertising segment has become a meaningful profit contributor. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026), with the stock gaining approximately 10% over that period — the weakest performer in the Pelosi 2026 exercise batch.

ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.

sources.title: Nancy Pelosi's 2026 Stock Moves — Motley Fool

ticker_meta.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
ticker_meta.blurb: Meta Platforms, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — collectively the largest social-media ecosystem in the world by monthly active users. The company generates the vast majority of its revenue through digital advertising, using detailed behavioural data to target ads across its platforms. After a painful 2022 in which shares fell roughly 65% amid a revenue slowdown and ballooning metaverse losses, Meta executed a dramatic turnaround by cutting costs, boosting margins, and rapidly integrating AI-driven ad ranking tools (Advantage+) that demonstrably improved advertiser returns. CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'Year of Efficiency' and the company followed through. By late 2025 Meta was simultaneously the most profitable it had ever been and the most aggressive in AI infrastructure spending, committing up to $65 billion in capex for 2025 and raising that figure to as much as $145 billion for 2026.
ticker_meta.recent: Meta reached an all-time high near $796 per share in September 2025. The stock declined approximately 24–28% from that peak through April 2026, with the primary investor concern being the scale of the 2026 capital-expenditure commitment — up to $145 billion — and uncertainty about whether AI-driven revenue would materialise at the pace required to justify it. Quarterly earnings remained strong through the period, but multiple compression drove share-price weakness.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.
